question: On 10 January 2025, the winner of the most recent elections in Venezuela took office. The National Electoral Council (CNE) named Nicolás Maduro the winner, with 51.95 % of the votes compared to Edmundo González Urrutia’s 43.18 %, although the CNE never published the records verifying those results.

A large part of the international community recognises Edmundo González as the winner of the last elections, including the G7 countries, the Organization of American States and institutions such as the European Parliament.

The opacity of the electoral process as a whole – and also in the publishing of the results – shows that what we are witnessing is unprecedented fraud that ends with the will expressed in the polls on 28 July 2024. 1.
Does the Commission believe that Nicolás Maduro can legitimately take office for a third time and not Edmundo González, as much of the international community claims?

Does the Commission intend to support further sanctions in the light of the continued acts of repression in the country, such as the kidnapping of opponents, including the son-in-law of Edmundo González?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.2.2025) On 28 July 2024, millions of Venezuelans voted for democratic change by supporting Edmundo González Urrutia by a significant majority, according to publicly available copies of electoral records (‘actas’). On several occasions, the EU has recalled its support to the Venezuelan people and to the upholding of democratic values1.

In choosing to disregard the will of the people and, instead, reinforcing repression against the population – including members of the democratic opposition and their families – Nicolás Maduro confirmed that he lacks the legitimacy of a democratically elected president.

In view of the situation in the country, on 9 January 2025 the Council decided to adopt a new package of targeted sanctions against 15 individuals responsible for undermining democracy, the rule of law or human rights in Venezuela2. Decisions and regulations on sanctions are adopted by the Council of the EU by unanimity.
These measures are targeted and flexible and can be scaled or reversed depending on progress made towards the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights in Venezuela.
